utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I must apologise that I caused a delay this morning in the start. Could we have the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fietelaars. If you'd be seated, please. If I could remind you of the affirmation that you took at the commencement which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Fietelaars. We're going to resume with the cross-examination and the questions I had for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown Document P138, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, would you please take a look at page 1 of the Dutch version, which is the second paragraph, and it begins with the words "Admiral Brovet."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether -- or rather what the position was of Admiral Brovet with respect to what was going on around the town of Dubrovnik at the material time described in this report; that is to say, the 23rd of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the text as given in the second page, it is quite correctly expressing my recollection of what took place. And I will read it for you: "Admiral Brovet's answers were in the same line as the ones he gave earlier that day to my second in command, it should be. The Croats are the ones who provoked the fighting, and the JNA only now and then fires back. It is the lack of goodwill of the Croats to cooperate, to reach a lasting agreement."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "Already ten times, a cease-fire was agreed, and six times the blockades should have been given up. But Tudjman does not do what he has signed. There are no barracks which have been liberated, and the result of 34 Croat attacks are 12 dead and 34 wounded on the JNA side."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression that Admiral Brovet was informed of the situation around the town of Dubrovnik at the time we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from him several times of the JNA position voice that most units of the Croatian army were located within the walls of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, within the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think it was specifically formulated like that. We talked about Dubrovnik, and we did not make all that large a difference between parts of the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But would you be so kind as to take a look at paragraph two -- the next paragraph of your report, where it says "Croatian units now have placed mortar units within the Dubrovnik walls."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was what was stated by Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what comparison did Admiral Brovet make with the burning of the Reichstag in that respect?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot put myself in Admiral Brovet's mind, but I think that what he wanted to express was that it was a plot by the other side to put the efforts towards peace of Admiral Brovet's side in a bad light.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself gain the impression that by explaining the events in this way, the events that were taking place in the Old Town of Dubrovnik and around it, Admiral Brovet, in fact, wished to tell you as the representative of the international community what his position was; that is to say, that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was a legitimate military target if, in fact, there were military forces located within it. Did you gain that impression?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not. Because Admiral Brovet expressly said that his forces were not part of an uncivilised country and that they were not in the business of destroying the cultural heritage of the nation. They had never fired on the old city, and they never would. That is what Admiral Brovet stated at different occasions. And I think he meant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown another document, please, P139.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the document and the portion which is marked "A". I think in the Dutch version, you will find that on page 1, the A section, because I would like to ask you a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in front of me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that in this particular conversation, Admiral Brovet clearly stated or indicated that everything that was happening around Dubrovnik was taking place pursuant to orders from the supreme command, or rather the presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Admiral Brovet personally indicate who represented the supreme command in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what he said, who Admiral Brovet mentioned as being the supreme commander in that situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was remaining body of the federal presidency which was presided by President Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now go on to Document P140, please. What position did Admiral Brovet express during this conversation with respect to the situation that the JNA found itself at the material time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I first make a side comment. This is a visit of my first collaborator, Mr. Hasselman, to Admiral Brovet, because I was otherwise employed. I signed off his draft, but I was not present at that conversation with Admiral Brovet. So whatever I say, I say on the authority of the report that Mr. Hasselman made to me. Would you please repeat the question, sir, because I've lost track.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please tell us what Admiral Brovet said to your associate with respect to the situation in which the JNA found itself on the territory of Croatia and generally in Yugoslavia at the time this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the admiral asked for understanding for the difficult position of the JNA which was a victim of false propaganda and information by the Croatian side. And Mr. Hasselman then brought forward that the source of the information that we received was Mr. Bondioli, the head of the EC monitor team present in Dubrovnik itself who were a witness of the activities in quotes -- that are quoted here in the second paragraph, "artillery fire on the edges of the city and shells dropping in the old harbour. And more recently tank fire from Obod to Zupa Bay area and heavy shelling of the outskirts of Dubrovnik city."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that. We'll read through that. All I'm asking you now is to tell me succinctly what his position was, and you have in fact answered that, and I thank you for your answer. Now, do you remember an example of exaggeration where propaganda came into play, where there was misrepresentation and information about the events around Vukovar, for example, Dubrovnik, and other military targets in Croatia at the time we're discussing, at the material time; that is to say, the last three months of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, sir. I did not look back at my notes on the situation in southern Slavonia, and Vukovar, and Osijek, and places like that because I assumed that that would not be material to this discussion -- these discussions. I can only say that I cannot judge the percentage of propaganda that was in the information of either side because (a), I went present there, and (b), I never made an effort to verify on the spot what conclusions could be drawn from visual evidence either in Vukovar or in Osijek. So I have no position on the thing -- the things that you are asking me now in this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of numerous cases in which the barracks were blocked, the JNA barracks in Croatia at that time where the water and electricity were switched off, cases where officers and soldiers were killed and kidnapped? I'm sure you'll remember that. I don't mean any specific case, but do you remember that things like that happened frequently during that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my conversations with Admiral Brovet, yes, you are right. He stated that this happened frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that your first immediate associate was told by Admiral Brovet, and you can find this on page 2 of the Dutch version of this report, that he actually enumerated all the cases of Croatian provocation in and around the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word "enumerate." He just mentioned a number of incidents, but he didn't describe the individual incidents. There's a statement about the quantity of incidents, rather than the incidents themselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the Dutch version, this will be the last line on page 1 and the beginning of page 2, does that list four cases on the 19th of October, on the 21st of October, once again on the 21st of October, and another incident. So four concrete, specific instances which your counsel was made aware of as examples, I assume, among all the other events and similar incidents that took place.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We noted that as a statement of Admiral Brovet, and we reported it as such. If you look at the grammar of the linea that we used, we said -- we used the verb declamation that in Dutch replaces the word "allegedly." In Dutch, the words are "zouden" and "zoud", which is "would have been" and "would." We took no position to the veracity of these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I didn't actually ask you that. But what I was asking you was whether the admiral did give and quote specific examples. Of course, you can't go into the veracity of them. You weren't able to do that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But neither did he describe the way in which fire was opened, whether it was heavy fire, whether it was fire by sidearms, whether it was fire by mortars, or whatever. That is what I meant when I said he mentioned the incidents, but he didn't describe the actual incidents as they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at the previous paragraph, you will see that Admiral Brovet says that "the JNA did not attack the town itself, despite Croatian provocations with that target in mind." And then he goes on to say, "the UNESCO team arriving in Dubrovnik will be able to establish that." And then Admiral Brovet goes on to say, "however, the Croats are trying to attract the fighting into town, and they have set mines in several locations, including the cultural monuments."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you read exactly what I assumed to be the statement of Admiral Brovet, which I reported faithfully to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the substance of the position taken by the supreme command of the JNA during the material time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness now, please, be shown another document. It is Exhibit 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But before we take a look at that exhibit, I should like to ask you to tell us how your visit came about, or rather how the idea for your visit first came about. And I'm talking about your visit of the 29th of October 1991 that you took part in, the visit to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the third lines under the heading message, you will see that the visit took place on the basis of an original contact of the second part of the week before the 29th between the Italian Ambassador and the vice minister for national defence in regards to Admiral Brovet in which the JNA offered to take the ambassadors of those countries that had been vocally critical of the behaviour of the JNA to the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us when Colonel Stojic briefed you with respect to the visit that was to take place.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the early morning of the 29th, before the flight to Tivat took off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you arrived in Tivat, where did Admiral Jokic receive you, if you remember. What kind of building was it, where was it? I mean, what type of building was it? A military barracks? Was it a headquarters? Was it a civilian building of some kind, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked like a military administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what did Admiral Jokic tell you about the nature of the conflict that was evolving at that time on the territory of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he repeated the allegations of Admiral Brovet that the whole conflict was caused and manipulated by Croatian extremists, and the other prong of his statement was that this series of incidents around Dubrovnik presented a real threat to the integrity of Montenegro for which -- and the military facilities in Montenegro which had to be protected by the JNA for strategic reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he perhaps mentioned some particular facilities that the JNA had to protect and that were in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Bay of Kotor and the facility at the exit of Prevlaka from the Bay of Kotor into the Adriatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did Admiral Jokic say who caused the conflict? Who provoked it, the one that is being talked about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He maintained that the whole conflict was caused by the Croatian extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he say then -- or rather, did he talk about a cowardly attack against a JNA facility at Prevlaka, about the occupation of strategic intersections?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, sir. He stated towards the end of his intervention that all the goals that the JNA had at the time of their preoccupation had now been reached, and there was no further need for military activities by the JNA unless Croatian provocations would resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he say that all the strategic intersections towards Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro were occupied and, as your report says, that all these provocations did make it incumbent upon the army, that is to say, the JNA, to react? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not if you use the present tense. I think he described that the strategic crossroads in that area had been occupied, and that the JNA had taken possession of those positions again, and that the action was satisfactory and objectives had been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did he say about taking JNA military facilities at the islands of Sipan and Mljet? What did he say about Kupari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that, again, is literally stated in these documents. This became really unavoidable, these JNA actions. When JNA officers were mistreated, families threatened and water, electricity, and supplies were cut off from the JNA facilities at Sipan, Mljet, and Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So all of that, all these events were mentioned by Admiral Brovet as the reason for the Dubrovnik operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they were not mentioned by Admiral Brovet. They were mentioned by Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then I misspoke. I wanted to ask whether those were the reasons that Admiral Jokic had mentioned as the reasons for the Dubrovnik operation. So your answer is yes, I gather?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Admiral Jokic said that there were other tasks that had to be completed? Did he say that the region should be cleansed and disarmed from Croatian paramilitaries? That's what he mentioned as the next task of the JNA. Isn't that correct? That is two paragraphs ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what was mentioned by Admiral Jokic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Admiral Jokic said that the tens of persons killed and the hundreds of persons wounded that the JNA had had in the Dubrovnik operation until then make it incumbent upon the military to act in that way? It's the same paragraph that you already dealt with a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the text. That is what the Admiral said, yes, that the JNA has no further objectives in the JNA area. There was no threat any more to the JNA. The only thing that still had to be done was to clear the region of all weapons and to make certain that the tens of dead and hundreds of wounded had not been sacrificed without cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic say how it was he intended to clean the region from these armed members of the Croatian forces, or did he only say what is mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we talked on about the way in which the JNA had executed the functions that it thought necessary in order to eliminate the sniper fire and find the caches of arms and to destroy them. And as far as possible, Admiral Jokic went on: "We preserved objects as well as we could."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was different. I'll try to rephrase it. Did it seem to you that Admiral Jokic's wish to clean the terrain of armed Croats could constitute an introduction to new conflicts that you, as the international community, were desperately trying to prevent?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think that that is a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to look at the following paragraph, below the one below the one we have just discussed. Did Admiral Jokic say there that not a single rifle was ever pointed at the Old Town? Did he tell you on the 29th of October that a single stone in Dubrovnik had never been touched?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did tell us that, sir, except when in the action for Kupari we were obliged to fire back at less important historic sites when they fired at us from the Hotel Belvedere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Later on, during the course of that day, did you see for yourself that Admiral Jokic had deceived you, or rather that he tried to deceive you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot put myself in the mind of Admiral Jokic about deception or not deception. One thing is certain, that we saw at least three pieces of damage which indicated that light mortar or artillery fire -- I'm no expert, so I cannot really judge that 100 per cent. Three instances of that kind of fire hit the Old Town. It was pointed out to us by the people who showed us around in the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, what Admiral Jokic said was not correct and was not truthful since you had seen with your very own eyes something that was not in line with what he had said. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to do it with 100 per cent precision, you're certainly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Admiral Jokic used the conditional here. He said "not a single rifle is pointed at the Old Town, nothing has been touched except when we had to return fire to historical sites of lesser importance." In this way, does Admiral Jokic allow for the possibility that under certain circumstances he could open fire at historical sites as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't know. We were talking about the old city of Dubrovnik. And then Admiral Jokic referred to less important historic sites. So I assume that he was not talking about the old city when he stated that he might be obliged to fire at it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can it be concluded on that basis that under certain circumstances, Admiral Jokic was ready to open fire at historic sites, too, historic sites of lesser or greater importance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. Speculation. Cannot answer for what Admiral Jokic would answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's a fair observation, Mr. Petrovic. You've, I think, got the ambassador as far as you might get him on this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at the next paragraph. Again, what Jokic was telling you, "there is no destruction of Dubrovnik. There will be none, depending on how soon we can find a final solution." Again, Admiral Jokic uses the conditional, if this is a proper translation, of course. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's referring to the destruction of Dubrovnik, not the destruction of the Old Town I assumed at the time. So -- and Dubrovnik was certainly damaged in the exercise of -- the activities of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he is putting conditions on the destruction of Dubrovnik in terms of the pace at which a final solution will be found?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're still talking within the context of that 100 per cent precision, he starts off with something that is not conditional. He says "there is no destruction of Dubrovnik. And there will be none." That's not a conditional. "There will be none" is an announcement of the future. "Depending on how fast we can find a solution," that is the time scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then please explain the following to me: If a solution cannot be found soon, then what is the substance of Jokic's answer?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask Admiral Jokic that. But I do not read in this sentence that if the final solution is delayed, that will cause a good argument to start damaging the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to explain the second half of your sentence to me. "Depending on how fast we can find a final solution," what was your understanding of that, of what Admiral Jokic had said?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a couple of sentences before the sentence we're talking about now, Admiral Jokic had stated that the objectives of the JNA had been achieved and that the Croats presented no danger any more to the JNA. So on that basis, there being no destruction of Dubrovnik, there being no threat from the Croats, and yet the objectives of the JNA having been achieved, those three things being true, I do not see any reason why the admiral would resume artillery activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you write this, then? "Depending on how fast we can find a final solution," I still do not understand what that means. What does that mean, "depending on how soon we can find a final solution"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, sir. You will see that there are quotation marks around most of these phrases. I just faithfully represent what Admiral Jokic has said. And if you want to know what went on in his mind when he said it, you should not address yourself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know why you wrote the second half of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I know why I wrote the second sentence. I wrote the second sentence because that was how Admiral Jokic expressed himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then, please, look at the following sentence, Jokic's sentence. "We cannot keep our combat units for a long time on these hills." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that Admiral Jokic was referring to supply problems for the people who were in military positions on the rim of the hills at the land side of Dubrovnik. But that's just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you say further on, again, you quote what Jokic said to you, "we cannot allow the members of the Croatian national guards corps to avoid surrender and the handover of weapons."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position that Admiral Jokic took. You skip one sentence, but I assume you did it on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on purpose. Look at the next sentence. Is that also in the conditional? "After that, that is to say, after the surrender, Dubrovnik will get electricity through Komolac and Plat." Is Admiral Jokic putting conditions here again, that Dubrovnik will get water and electricity if there is a surrender?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, sir. That's a condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these the conditions? Is this the conditional that we see in the first sentence of this paragraph, the one that we tried to discuss a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the conditional means that the JNA will stop making the situation in Dubrovnik unlivable for the civilian population if the military and irregular Croat national guards surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion from all of this, if I may say so, could have only been the following: Regardless of what Admiral Jokic says, he intends to continue military operations until there is a full surrender of the members of the National Guards Corps. How else can he achieve what it says here that he said to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what goes on in the mind of leading people in those situations. And if you look a bit further down, after the ambassadors came back, you will see that we refer to exactly the same situation where we feel that notwithstanding the positions expressed in these linea, to us it's incomprehensible and unthinkable that a civilian population is held hostage by refusing them water and food and holding them hostage in a situation that is very dangerous unless the military people in that same area surrender and give up their weapons. The civilian population should be protected under those circumstances, according to all precepts of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Were you concerned over what you had heard from Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was concerned about the situation, not only about what I heard from Admiral Jokic. I was concerned about what I heard from any sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was General Bondioli? Was General Bondioli the head of the monitoring mission of the European community for the entire region?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, there is no evidence that there is a General Bondioli. That term has never been used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Bondioli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Ambassador Bondioli.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course it's not. I'm sorry. Mr. Bondioli. Is it correct that Mr. Bondioli was head of the regional centre of the monitoring mission for the entire region of Dalmatia, including southern Dalmatia, or rather, the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was. And he was resident in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to Mr. Bondioli about the situation in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: By the very nature of his mission, was Mr. Bondioli the person who was the best versed in developments concerning Dubrovnik from among the members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see it as a competition between better versed and lesser versed. But Mr. Bondioli was a good source of information to the embassy in its -- in its persona as representing the presidency of the European Union for which Mr. Bondioli and the European monitoring mission worked. So it was a logical chain of reporting for Mr. Bondioli, and it was a logical source of information for me. But there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Bondioli said to you that he had concluded that all substantive decisions that are made concerning Dubrovnik are taken by General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Such remark as far as I'm concerned was never made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask for us to take the first morning break now, if possible, if you agree. I would have to ask you this for the reasons that I explained to your legal officer. If you allow this, I would like to express my great thanks and also my apology to any inconvenience this may cause to you, Your Honours, to the Prosecution, and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Petrovic, you may need half an hour or 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're appearing before another Chamber or in a conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and take a longer break. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we'll await your return.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise once again for this major inconvenience that I've caused in this way to you and to everyone in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That delay was much longer than we anticipated, but we seem to be all together again. Sorry to have kept you waiting, Mr. Fietelaars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never mind, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And once again, thank you very much for your understanding. I should like to have the witness shown the document that we mentioned before the break; that is to say, P141.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that Mr. Bondioli conveyed his feelings, that is to say, that he thought that Admiral Jokic was a stronghand man, hardliner, and full sympathiser of the policy wage?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the discussions and then the exchange of information with Mr. Bondioli didn't specifically touch upon that point. I'm sure that both Mr. Bondioli and I agreed that the high JNA officers weren't loyal to the policies that the JNA wanted to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I just want to point out that the passage that is in -- at least my document says that on page -- it would be the third page of the exhibit, he had the feeling that Jokic was the "real hardliner" and that Strugar was "just a military man". It doesn't say anything about the full support of the policy waged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That certainly accords with the document in the English language, Ms. Somers. But I think the transcript having reflected that, we've moved on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to tell me whether it is right that Mr. Bondioli told him that it was his impression that Admiral Jokic was a hardliner.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your impression was that Admiral Jokic was a hardliner. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that Admiral Jokic was representing a point of view in which he believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does the word "hardliner" mean? How do you understand the word that "Jokic was the real hardliner"? What does real hardliner actually mean in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my vocabulary, hardliner means that somebody is 100 per cent behind the point of view that he represents, without exception and without conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it right that about Strugar, it was said "just a military man"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression that the gentleman who was standing next to Admiral Jokic did listen in very carefully, but did not participate in the discussion, and that therefore I understood that the policy there was represented by Admiral Jokic and by Admiral Jokic only, given the fact that the other gentleman didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The conclusions about that, that is to say, that Jokic was a real hardliner and that Strugar was "just a military man," are they your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, take a look in Document P141, page 3 of that document, last paragraph there, 141 is the document in front of you, sir. It is P141. So page 3 of that document that is before you, the last paragraph on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And it begins with "Mr. Bondioli said..."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You're right. And it came up in the discussion. And I'm really not quite certain whether I reached the conclusions and Mr. Bondioli confirmed them, or that Mr. Bondioli used that kind of wording and then I confirmed it. But given the fact that -- what it says here, I certainly want to change my statement in saying that it probably was -- the wording probably was introduced by Mr. Bondioli in a discussion with me. And I apologise for not remembering this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can agree that both your impressions and those of Mr. Bondioli were, as far as Mr. Jokic was concerned, was that he was indeed a real hardliner. We can deduce that, can we not, from what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the definition that I just gave to you on your request, yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, you told us, if I remember correctly, that Mr. Bondioli had not arrived at the conclusion that the real decisions with respect to Dubrovnik were taken by General Kadijevic. Now, when you look at this paragraph again, do you stand by that assertion? Or do you think that in actual fact, your position at the time and your report were different?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The first line in that linea represents the point of view of Mr. Bondioli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read. "Mr. Bondioli said that from his negotiations, Admiral Jokic and General Pavle Strugar, he concluded" --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bondioli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: -- "that the real decisions affecting Dubrovnik were being made by General Kadijevic."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that I'm a little confused now as to what is correct. Is it true and correct that Mr. Bondioli told you that it was his conclusion that all the decisions affecting Dubrovnik were made by Kadijevic? Would that be correct? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the decisions, the real decisions in the sense of the major decisions. I don't think that tactical decisions on small-scale events would have -- could have come from Belgrade. And you are correct, sir; this is the conclusion that Mr. Bondioli said he reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us on what grounds you yourself were able to conclude that Jokic was a hardliner and whether certain details to that effect were conveyed to you by Mr. Bondioli at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Bondioli spoke on the basis of his own negotiations in the previous days and weeks with the gentlemen concerned. And my confirmation in this report of that kind of opinion is based rather on the discussion that we had in the evening after our visit to Dubrovnik itself when we went back to Tivat and had our talk with the gentlemen who received us upon us coming back. And as I said, one was silent most of the time, but listened in. And the other one was Admiral Jokic. And that confirmed very much that there was no light between the formal decisions of the JNA and his own convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether it is correct that on that day, when you were in Tivat, nobody introduced General Strugar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came back from -- excuse me. When we came back from Dubrovnik, we were received in the same place as where we arrived that morning. There were two -- there were two high-ranking gentlemen that we spoke to through interpreters. And the names were never mentioned. As I said before yesterday, Admiral Jokic I recognised, and the other gentleman I hadn't seen before and I hadn't seen since.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see him here today in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man that I hadn't seen before and I hadn't seen since, it means that I only saw him one time. After 14 -- almost 14 years, no, I would not confirm that the face that you refer to is the face of the same gentleman that was at that party. I simply can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your opinion that it might perhaps have been General Strugar is nothing other than your assumption on the basis of what you expected to see and what you were told that morning in Belgrade. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not on the basis of what I expected to see, but what we were told by Colonel Stojic, that in the course of the day we would see Admiral Jokic and General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And nothing other than that indicated to you that perhaps it really was General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it was nothing more than an assumption on your part which was deduced from what you had heard that morning from Colonel Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it could have been any other officer of the JNA at the reception, the person who you thought might have been General Strugar? Could it have been any other officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, yes. But in practice, I would have expected somebody to point out to us that General Strugar, although announced, was at that moment not available. That didn't happen. So my assumption, as you call it, remained what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the official report to your government, you don't mention by a single word the fact that you had a meeting with General Strugar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. And that was because the same considerations that I have just put forward also occurred to me while I was writing -- while I was reading the first draft of this report, which is the reason why I wrote that line at the bottom which says "I think General Strugar was present also." Because by that time, but it was after we returned to Belgrade, I started to doubt whether I should use that name, yes or no. So as you see in my report, I changed it upon the phrase "Admiral Jokic and his staff..." And in there assuming that the admiral, because of the fact that he was the only one who spoke, was the number one of the company that we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You weren't sure then or now that the man you saw standing beside General Jokic was in fact General Strugar. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pencilled-in note that appears at the bottom of the page was pencilled in on the 30th of October when I went through my draft, as it lies here. And in the draft that went to the communications room in the embassy, the original text had been changed by me before reaching. I think. But that, again, it's also 13, 14 years ago. I probably had said something upon the gentlemen concerned or upon the officers concerned, and then realising that if I was asked for absolutely authentic identification of one of the two, that I would not have been able to describe that. So that is the reason for the pencilled-in note, I think. And that is why I changed this -- in the original draft, I changed "the officers concerned," or phrases to that effect, and I put in "Admiral Jokic and his staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that a little later in due course. But let me go back now to your visit to the Old Town itself. How frequently did you have contacts with the mayor of Dubrovnik, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he telephoned me with information that he thought would be useful to the Netherlands Embassy or to the presidency of the European Union Embassies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what he told you? What did his -- the gist of his conversation sound to you like?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was a besieged city in which a number of people were so afraid that they wanted to flee, and a number of people that hardened their positions because they wanted to protect the place where they had lived for generations. And moreover, the fact whether the shelling or the activity from the outside waxed or waned. We also heard in the context of cease-fires whether or not they were in his point of view respected by the JNA. And all the time he confirmed that from the Croatian side, no activity was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you about the hundreds of shells that were falling on the Old Town at the time? Perhaps he exaggerated to you, too, like he did to the media and others, saying that 15.000 shells fell on Dubrovnik and its Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well be true that 15.000 shells fell on Dubrovnik and its Old Town, but they certainly didn't fall on the Old Town. Because by the time of 29th of October, well in the afternoon, we only could confirm three strikes within the Old Town of what we assumed was mortar fire. And that was all. But that is only referring to the Old Town, not to the suburbs and the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this: Did that man already at that time, that is to say in October, prior to your visit claim that hundreds, if not thousands, of shells fell on -- had fallen on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he certainly didn't. He talked about increased pressure. And as I said, waning pressure. And it may well be that in discussions with my military attache, this kind of military information came up, but not in conversations with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any rumours going round or reports or propaganda on the part of the Croatian side and Croatian government with respect to this issue, saying that there were thousands or tens of thousands of shells raining into the Old Town of Dubrovnik? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The embassies of the European Union all had their contacts with Dubrovnik, and they were certainly not under the impression that that which you just described took place. It may well be that the population of Belgrade under the influence of Belgrade television believed that. But the embassies certainly didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you arrived, when you came to Dubrovnik, you noticed damages on several buildings. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we noticed damages to three buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, which those three buildings were that were damaged and that you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were identified to us by the people who received us upon arrival on Venetian quay on the Old Town of Dubrovnik. The one was the bell tower. The other one was a library. And the third one was a pharmacy. The bell tower had been sit on the side. I myself saw one hole, and some black streaks around the hole indicating that the hole was the consequence of an explosion. And we saw two roofs which had lost a number of their roofing tiles and through which we could see damaged beams that had supported the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned three damages.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, the pharmacy and the library, were they within the complex of the Franciscan monastery, within that compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know, sir. We walked by. We saw two roofs and they were pointed out to us. But we never looked at the map for the location, let alone the ownership of the two buildings concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can jog your memory in this way, refresh it: Those two buildings, the library and the pharmacy, are they at the bottom of the main street looking at it from the port where you disembarked, going that way? Would they be at the end of that main street? Does that refresh your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that 100 per cent. But it appears to me that coming from the bell tower into the street, that they were at the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A little further off, quite a way from the bell tower, for example, 100 to 150 metres on your right from the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, whether it was a hundred or 200 or 250 metres. We walked talking in that direction, and I didn't pace my steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But it is several hundred metres roughly.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The length of that street is several hundred metres, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Document P31, now, please. [In English] Yes, you can put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, please, take a look at the document, Mr. Fietelaars, and tell me whether that is indeed the bell tower, the picture. Is it indeed the bell tower and the damage that you have described?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it is not, as far as my recollection is concerned. If I could see a picture of the whole length of the tower, then maybe you would make it easier to me to recognise it. The damage I saw at least was not at a -- on a dome on top of the thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing the photograph any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why did Jokic tell you to return from Dubrovnik before 1630 hours that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic told us that it was for our own protection because of sniper fire from the shore that was not yet under control of the JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you about any sniper fire that could be targeting a plane, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. He said that the plane should take off before dark because otherwise it would be too dangerous to fly. I don't know on what part of the flight the danger that he saw would appear or not appear, whether it would be sniper fire or gunfire of another nature. It didn't come up. It only was mentioned that it was too dangerous to go -- to go back in the dark, and it was too dangerous to fly in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, did you give a statement to the officer of the OTP on the 21st of January of this year?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir. On the 21st of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 21st of January this year; that is to say, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the Office of the Prosecution before. But I don't -- I know that I made a statement, but I don't know that it was on the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a written statement at any stage of your contacts with the Prosecution? Did you make any statements to the gentlemen of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a conversation with two gentlemen of the Prosecution. And they noted down what I -- they had questions. They noted down what I said. And I put my signature below it because my answers to their questions were approximately what they had put on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you read what they wrote?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they correctly record what you had said?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if I would have written it, it would have been different. But this statement was not taken while in the offices of the Prosecution. It was taken at my home in the Netherlands by two visiting officers of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any objections regarding the accuracy of some of the things that are referred to in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have talked to the Prosecutors since in the preparation for this meeting. And I think that a document now exists which supersedes the document at that time because improvements in the rendering of my recollection have been made in that document. Therefore, the first document is of no consequence any more as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please help me understand this: When did you sign a statement to the gentlemen of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of their visit to my home in 'S-Hertogenbosch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was this, Mr. Fietelaars?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember the date, but it was somewhere the end of January or the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you did give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in which you described everything to the best of your recollection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement to two gentlemen of the Offices of the Prosecutor. And they recorded what they thought I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the question regarding Jokic and the trip. You said something to us a few moments ago that is decidedly different to what you said in the statement. In paragraph 16, it says: "He instructed us to return before 4.30 because after it -- after dark, he could not guarantee aircraft safety. It would be prone, as he claimed, to sniper fire."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But that's exactly what I said. It would be prone to sniper fire, not necessarily sniper fire at the takeoff. There was a whole flight to Belgrade, and he did not say what kind of sniper fire there could or would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of aircraft was it that you flew on that could be subject to sniper fire during its flight, Mr. Fietelaars?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew what type of aircraft it was, but I didn't know whether it could be subject to sniper fire. That was up to Admiral Jokic. It was a 50-seater passenger plane of Russian fabrication -- manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting in the area where your plane was supposed to take off from?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the area around Dubrovnik, so it was full of JNA troops. Tivat itself, I think, is a base with -- where a lot of military activity takes place. The Bay of Kotor is near, Prevlaka is near. So there may very well are military activity. But I don't know whether at that time that military activity at that moment was movement or fighting or anything. We didn't see it. We were not allowed to travel along land because that was too dangerous according to Admiral Jokic. We did go by launch to Dubrovnik. We were not allowed to go by buses to Dubrovnik. And we were picked up again by launch at Dubrovnik. We transferred to a much faster boat --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you something, Mr. Ambassador. If you can, could you please keep your answers shorter. Could you only answer the questions that I have. Otherwise, we will all stay here for a very long time. My question was simply: Was there any fighting in the area that your aircraft was supposed to take off from? Yes or no. Or can this not be explained at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything? Did you hear gunfire in Tivat?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away is Tivat from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two-and-a-half hours by slow launch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's far away, very far away?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on your judgement for what far away is. It took two-and-a-half hours to get there by slow launch, and it took one hour to come back by fast launch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: 60 or 70 kilometres away? That's far away, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Dubrovnik, who pointed out the JNA positions to you, the JNA positions around the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, there was a lot of activity visible from the ramparts of the Old Town in the hills. Now, on the rim of the hills. And furthermore Mr. Bondioli, the mayor of Dubrovnik, and the representative of the Croatian government in Zagreb, they pointed out the disposition of the different gun placements and troop concentrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said to us yesterday that outside the Old Town, you saw some houses that were destroyed. So you came to the conclusion that in those houses, there certainly could not have been any military activity, or any reason why they would have been destroyed or damaged or set on fire. How could you conclude that? You saw what you saw, but what happened before or after is something that you had no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but we were assured of the gentlemen who accompanied us that there was no military activity in that area, nor did we see any, nor did we see anybody with arms that could not for the same money be a policeman. So hundreds of troops or thousands of troops were certainly not seen by any of us. It is maybe half a dozen of people, but not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And where was it that you saw these people?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road, in the suburbs, helping out with clearing damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the Croatian forces at all in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the differences in uniform were, but as I said I saw maybe half a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see whether they were armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had sidearms, some had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anything else regarding Croatian military presence in the Old Town of Dubrovnik and in the town of Dubrovnik itself during your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they point out the Croatian positions to you as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask where the positions of the other side in this conflict were?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We walked around in the Old Town and in the damaged part of the new town, and we saw no military activity. That's the limit of my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you asked where the positions of the Croatian side were, or were you not interested in that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two questions. Which one do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask where the positions of the Croatian side were first of all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why were you not interested in that, since that was indispensable for you in order to have a complete picture of what was going on in the area that you had come to visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not acknowledge that that question is a viable one because the Dubrovnik authorities showed us around in the Old Town and in the new town. We saw nothing, so we had no reason to ask any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are in an armed conflict zone. Did you wonder who was clashing with who there? Isn't that the first thing that you should have been interested in?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you define it as an armed conflict zone. We defined it as a zone where a city with a civilian population was besieged by an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this town defended?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so far as we could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As an ambassador during those three months of 1991, did you hear that the town was being defended?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, there was -- as far as our information that came out of the city was concerned, there was a low level of defence. But very soon, the pressure on the civilian population was so big that they started to leave, and a number of people who you define as troops or irregulars or maybe even Croatian JNA people who were still in the city and did want to escape from the fighting, that they left with the civilian population. But I saw nothing that indicated that there was a garrison or a military force in the Old Town, nor in the direct surrounds of the Old Town outside the ramparts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was whether during the last three months of 1991 you heard that Dubrovnik was defended by Croatian forces. Yes or no? Or was it an undefended town under siege? How would you define the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I defined it in my previous answer. A low level of defence by very few people. That was the information that reached us. And also, that people started to leave, mainly civilian population, but they may have been interspersed by young people who wanted to escape capture. That was the information we received, and that is what I indicated in my previous reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This low level of defence, how did you find out about it, about that particular level of defence? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly from Mr. Bondioli and a number of Dutch journalists who resided or stayed in Dubrovnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like later, in November and December that year?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as I can recollect, the pressure on the civilian population increased. And a number of people, and in some of the documents, I think I even related numbers that I heard from Bondioli, numbers of people who actually left by ferry to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you do not understand me well. I have been asking you the following: If that was the situation with the Croatian military forces in October, the way you described it, what was the Croatian military presence in Dubrovnik in November and December then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I have not visited Dubrovnik in that period. I had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. depend on telephone information and general information received by sources that are accessible to all and the things that were stated by the representatives of the JNA in Belgrade. That packet of information led me to the conclusion that more and more people, including military -- young men with military activities, were leaving and had left Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So according to the information you had, the defence of Dubrovnik was becoming weaker and weaker. What existed in October was no longer there in December, because people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what was there in October was already practically invisible to a visitor to Dubrovnik who had all freedom to walk the streets, both of the Old Town and the new town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The level of Dubrovnik that -- the level of defence in Dubrovnik that existed in October, according to the information you had, was it getting lower and lower? Was there less and less of it in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: More and more people had left, including young people. So I assume, and as I said, it's a conclusion that I reached, that it was getting lower and lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is the information that you had at the time, so this is the information that you conveyed to the government of the Kingdom of the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the information I had at the time augmented with the conclusions that I drew out of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And that is the information that you conveyed to the government of your country, or rather, the countries of the European Union?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the Presidency of the European Union, which in that period was the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and all my correspondence went to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, on the basis of such reports of yours, was the official policy of the government of your country and other countries of the European Union built on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not built on that because it only had the pretense to reflect the actual situation in the country, and not political developments going on in our own countries. That is the political responsibility of the minister, and not of his servants abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the entire policy was not built on that basis, then the position in terms of what was going on in and around Dubrovnik, what was going on, in fact - I'm not referring to major policy - was that based inter alia on what you reported to your government and to the European Union?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it was one of the building stones that they used, just as there are others, like the reports of the monitoring mission, Ambassador van Houten, Ambassador Wijnaendts, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that their reports contained the same type and quality of information like the reports you sent to your government and to the European Commission in good faith?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were done by a similar type of professional diplomat as I am. I don't want to judge the quality of my own work, nor do I want to judge the quality of the work of my colleagues. But every ambassador in Belgrade made his reports also to his own government in the meetings between foreign ministers of the European Union, those snippets of information emanating from all the embassies were brought into the discussion. So it was a whole kaleidoscopic group of information in fact that formed the basis of the considerations and the decisions of the foreign ministers in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But your building block of information was a shade more important because at that time your country was presiding over the European Union. Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious, sir, that you don't know how that functions. Everybody considers his own information the most important. The British government considers the information that they have received the most important. All these things were put together, and a formal conclusion was reached. But it is not that a report of the presidency carries far greater weight in discussions in Brussels. The presidency report only makes certain that all capitals know the opinion of the presidency. At the same time and as quickly after the date that it happened as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed by your ministry that your information was not in accordance with the information provided by the other member countries of the European Union?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My minister is not in use - in the habit of writing that kind of notes. Every time you travel to your bases, you have a conversation with him. And then those things may come up. I had never had occasion to be ashamed of what I wrote, and he has, in my recollection at least, never found occasion to chide me because of the low quality of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were never any objections as regards the accuracy of your reports in the period that we are discussing now. Of course, I'm not asking about your entire career; I'm asking about the period that is relevant to us here.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a relationship of trust between Dutch ministers of their ambassadors. If that relationship of trust is broken, the ambassador is removed. I've never been removed from a posting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the ambassadors of other western countries accredited in Belgrade over these three months that we are discussing now?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any of them have different information regarding what was going on in Dubrovnik in relation to the information that you had and that you had sent to your foreign ministry?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But most embassies had additional information rather than different informations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The fundamental tone of the information was the same, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be the judge of that. I know the tone of the things that I wrote. But I never saw copies of the reports that the individual ambassadors made to their capitals unless they came by my office and wanted to discuss it. So on the whole, no, I do not know that -- whether their tone was fundamentally the same as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to Dubrovnik yet again now. Is it correct that Admiral Jokic restricted the duration of your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that they returned you from Dubrovnik to Tivat on a fast boat, and this was something that bordered on lack of respect for ambassadors from different countries accredited to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You assume incorrectly, that that would be insulting. It wouldn't. It was an exciting thing to travel by fast boat, so we would have enjoyed it if we could have boarded from the quay on to that boat. However, we were taken out by the launch to mid sea. And while both boats were travelling, we were transferred from one to the other. We had some elderly gentlemen with us who had great difficulty getting from one boat to the other and who hit their shins against the sides of the boat. And it was all a very ungraceful exercise. That was a source of irritation, but not the fact that we used a fast boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 17, you say --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have the document in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have a copy here. But I'm going to read it out to you, and my colleague will intervene if I read something out that differs from what it says in the document. I do not intend to tender the document into evidence, but this is what it says in paragraph 17: "The crew of the motorboat told us that they would take us to Tivat at high-speed. When the vessel arrived at sea, we were transferred roughly and dangerously. We felt intimidated by this because it introduced an unnecessary sense of urgency." That is what you said on the 21st of January this year.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, what I read out to you just now?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that they were rough; that they transferred you dangerously and that you were intimidated?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly felt intimidated because at my age I do not like to step from one boat in another going even at a slow speed and the waves crashing and hitting my shins from one boat to the other, with the danger of getting between the two. We are not sailors, and we are not people who are on a pleasure cruise or on that kind of activity. I felt it was dangerous. I felt it was rough. And I felt personally intimidated because I feared falling in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this attitude taken towards you because you violated what Jokic said to you, because you stayed in Dubrovnik longer than he had told you to stay?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. I don't have that information. If it is because of that that they took this action, then you should find out by the people who made the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about your impression. Was it your impression --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "tell me was this attitude taken towards you because..."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question. Was it your impression that they were rough to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. Speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe it is speculative, Your Honour, to phrase it from that perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. By your leave. By your leave, I am interested in what the witness thought, what his impression was, not what somebody else thought and what somebody else decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
